items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.

items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.

items.title: sin(1 degree) is irrational
items.claim: Sine of 30°, 45°, 60° are simple expressions like 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2. Sine of 1 degree, 7 degrees, or most other 'nice' integer degree values are irrational numbers with no closed elementary form.
items.prompt: Why are most integer-degree sine values irrational?

options.text: Niven's theorem (1956): the only rational values of sin(theta) for rational theta in degrees occur at multiples of 30 (giving sin = 0, plus/minus 1/2, plus/minus 1). Almost all other rational-degree sines are irrational

items.reveal_title: Niven's theorem and the gaps in trigonometric tables
items.reveal:
Ivan Niven (1956) proved: if both theta (in degrees) and sin(theta) are rational, then sin(theta) is 0, ±1/2, or ±1. By similar argument, cos(theta) rational with theta rational forces cos(theta) in {0, ±1/2, ±1, ±sqrt(2)/2... wait — Niven's actual statement covers SINES specifically}.

The consequence: sin(1°), sin(2°), sin(3°), ... are mostly irrational. Specifically, the standard table of integer-degree sines contains only a few rational values: sin(0°) = 0, sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(90°) = 1, and their reflections (150°, 210°, 270°, 330°). Every other entry in the table is irrational.

This is one reason the SPECIAL ANGLES (30°, 45°, 60°) feature so heavily in geometry: they have simple exact values. Most other angles need decimal approximations.

Closed-form expressions: many integer-degree sines do have closed forms in terms of nested radicals — they're algebraic numbers — but the expressions are ugly. For example, sin(15°) = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4. sin(18°) = (sqrt(5) - 1)/4 (related to the regular pentagon).

For sin(1°): expressible in radicals (it's algebraic, a root of an integer polynomial) but the expression has dozens of nested terms. Modern algebra has tools to compute it exactly; it's just not a useful form.

Why 30° and 45° are special: regular hexagons (60° angles) and squares (45°) tile the plane with simple geometric constructions; the corresponding sine/cosine values come out as simple radicals.

Gauss and constructibility: a regular n-gon is constructible with compass and straightedge if and only if n is a product of powers of 2 and distinct Fermat primes (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537). This is why the 17-gon is constructible (Gauss's first major result, age 19) but the 7-gon and 9-gon aren't.
items.why: Trigonometric tables look like they could be filled with simple values. Almost all entries are deeply irrational, expressible only in nested radicals or numerical approximations. The 'special angles' of school maths are a tiny privileged set.
